note: Teaching model written for the site. Starting point: A$1 = US 70 cents, reserves US$60 billion. Numbers are illustrative, not real data.

systems.name: Floating
systems.who: Demand and supply in the foreign exchange market, minute by minute.
systems.bank: Normally nothing. It keeps reserves but does not use them to steer the rate.
systems.reserves: Small: reserves are not needed to defend a rate.
systems.money: Full independence: the central bank can set interest rates for domestic goals such as inflation.
pros: The rate adjusts by itself to shocks, acting as a shock absorber for the economy
Monetary policy is free to target inflation and employment
No need to hold large reserves; speculators have no fixed rate to attack
cons: The rate can be volatile, creating uncertainty for exporters, importers and borrowers
A falling currency raises import prices and the cost of foreign-currency debt
The rate can overshoot what the fundamentals justify
systems.examples: Australia since December 1983; the United States, Japan, the United Kingdom, the euro area.

systems.name: Managed float
systems.short: The market sets the rate, the central bank smooths it
systems.who: Mostly the market, but the central bank buys or sells its currency to slow large or disorderly moves. Also called a dirty float.
systems.bank: Leans against the wind: buys its own currency when it is falling fast and sells it when it is rising fast.
systems.reserves: Moderate: enough to intervene from time to time.
systems.money: Mostly independent, although heavy intervention affects the money supply unless it is offset (sterilised).
pros: Keeps most of the shock-absorbing benefit of a float
Reduces sharp swings that damage confidence and trade
Buys time for exporters, importers and borrowers to adjust
cons: Intervention only delays an adjustment that the fundamentals require
Uses up reserves if the central bank fights a persistent trend
It can be unclear what the central bank is aiming for
systems.examples: Many emerging economies, such as India and Indonesia. The Reserve Bank of Australia has intervened occasionally, for example when the market became disorderly in 2008.

systems.name: Flexible peg
systems.short: A fixed rate that the authorities reset when pressure builds
systems.who: The government or central bank announces a rate (the peg) and defends it, but changes the peg when it is clearly out of line with the market.
systems.bank: Buys or sells its currency every day to hold the peg, then devalues or revalues to a new peg when the gap becomes too large.
systems.reserves: Large: needed to hold the peg between adjustments.
systems.money: Limited: defending the peg changes the money supply, and interest rates may have to be used to protect the currency.
pros: More certainty for trade and investment than a float, most of the time
The peg can be moved, so a serious misalignment does not have to last
Less risk of running out of reserves than a rigid fixed rate
cons: Adjustments come as sudden jumps (devaluations or revaluations) rather than gradual moves
Speculators can profit by betting on the next adjustment, which adds to the pressure
Between adjustments the economy carries the cost of the wrong exchange rate
systems.examples: Australia before the float: pegged to the US dollar from 1971, to a trade-weighted basket from 1974, and adjusted daily (a crawling peg) from 1976 to 1983.

systems.name: Fixed
systems.short: The authorities hold one rate whatever happens
systems.who: The government or central bank sets the rate and commits to keeping it.
systems.bank: Buys or sells whatever amount of its currency is needed to hold the rate, for as long as it has the reserves to do so.
systems.reserves: Very large: the rate lasts only as long as the reserves do.
systems.money: Almost none: the money supply and interest rates must follow whatever is needed to hold the rate.
pros: Certainty for exporters, importers and investors
Can anchor inflation if the currency is fixed to a low-inflation currency
Removes exchange rate speculation while the rate is credible
cons: The rate cannot absorb shocks, so output and jobs adjust instead
Monetary policy cannot be used for domestic goals
If reserves run out the rate collapses in a currency crisis
systems.examples: Hong Kong (to the US dollar since 1983), Saudi Arabia and other Gulf states (to the US dollar), Denmark (to the euro).

shocks.name: Commodity prices rise
shocks.why: Foreign buyers need more Australian dollars to pay for dearer exports, so demand for the dollar increases.

shocks.name: Global downturn
shocks.why: Trading partners buy fewer Australian exports, so demand for the dollar decreases.

shocks.name: Australian interest rates rise relative to overseas
shocks.why: Foreign savers buy Australian dollars to earn the higher return (demand increases) and Australians keep more funds at home (supply decreases).

shocks.name: Overseas interest rates rise relative to Australia
shocks.why: Funds move overseas for the higher return: demand for the dollar decreases and supply increases.

shocks.name: Australians buy more imports
shocks.why: Importers sell Australian dollars to buy foreign currency, so the supply of the dollar increases.

shocks.name: Speculators expect the dollar to fall
shocks.why: Speculators sell Australian dollars now and buyers hold off, so supply increases and demand decreases.

shocks.name: Foreign investment boom
shocks.why: Foreign firms buy Australian dollars to invest in Australia, so demand for the dollar increases.

shocks.name: Higher inflation in Australia than overseas
shocks.why: Australian goods become less competitive: exports fall (demand decreases) and imports rise (supply increases).

shocks.name: Let a period pass with no new shock
shocks.why: Nothing new happens. Watch what continues to change under each system.

timeline.detail: The Australian currency was fixed to sterling, and through it to the US dollar under the Bretton Woods system of fixed rates.
As Bretton Woods broke down, the peg was moved from sterling to the US dollar.
The dollar was pegged to a basket of trading partners' currencies (the origin of the Trade Weighted Index) rather than to one currency.
After a large devaluation in November 1976, the peg was reviewed and adjusted frequently by a small group of officials. This was a flexible peg.
With large capital flows making the peg impossible to manage, the government floated the dollar and removed most exchange controls.
The market sets the rate. The Reserve Bank has intervened at times when the market was disorderly, for example in 2008, but does not target a level.
